pages.text: Doris’s Uncle Opare lived in a mining town and dug for gold with five friends. Each of them worked his own small pit. When a vehicle came down the road, they scattered. “We are not thieves,” Uncle Opare told her at the house one evening. “We are hungry men with no papers.” Doris looked at his rough hands. “Uncle, why do you not work as one group?” she asked. He laughed sadly. “Because the paper is too hard,” he said.
sentences: Doris’s Uncle Opare lived in a mining town and dug for gold with five friends.
Each of them worked his own small pit.
When a vehicle came down the road, they scattered.
“We are not thieves,” Uncle Opare told her at the house one evening.
“We are hungry men with no papers.” Doris looked at his rough hands.
“Uncle, why do you not work as one group?” she asked.
He laughed sadly.
“Because the paper is too hard,” he said.
pages.alt: A girl and her uncle sit outside a house at dusk, with rubber boots by the door.

pages.text: The next day, Doris asked her social studies teacher, Mr Nunoo, about the paper. “Good question,” he said. “Under the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006, a person needs a small-scale mining licence. The land is limited to twenty-five acres. According to a legal guide, the applicant must be a Ghanaian citizen of at least eighteen years, registered with the Minerals Commission’s district office. Licences may also go to cooperatives. A cooperative is a group that owns a business together.”

According to a legal guide, the applicant must be a Ghanaian citizen of at least eighteen years, registered with the Minerals Commission’s district office.
Licences may also go to cooperatives.
A cooperative is a group that owns a business together.”
pages.alt: A teacher holds up a printed law beside a map with a small square marked on it.

pages.text: “How does it work?” she asked. Mr Nunoo counted on his fingers. “The applicant goes to the district office of the Minerals Commission. The application is sent on and published in the gazette, the official government notice. Chiefs and traditional authorities are told and can give their views. The Minister decides. A first licence lasts up to five years. But fees, forms and rules change, and the guide does not list every document, so always ask the district office. It will also tell you about other approvals, such as environmental ones.”

pages.text: “Is there help for groups?” asked Doris. “In August 2025,” said Mr Nunoo, “Cabinet approved a programme called rCOMSDEP, the Responsible Cooperative Mining and Skills Development Programme. According to the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, it promotes locally owned mining cooperatives, with legal concessions, training and shared processing centres with modern gold recovery and water treatment. It also plans to phase out mercury and restore land. But the published pages do not say how to join, so ask.”

“In August 2025,” said Mr Nunoo, “Cabinet approved a programme called rCOMSDEP, the Responsible Cooperative Mining and Skills Development Programme.

According to the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, it promotes locally owned mining cooperatives, with legal concessions, training and shared processing centres with modern gold recovery and water treatment.
It also plans to phase out mercury and restore land.
But the published pages do not say how to join, so ask.”
pages.alt: A teacher points to a poster of a shared processing centre with clean water tanks.

pages.text: “And the gold?” asked Doris. “Selling is also governed by law,” said Mr Nunoo. “Under the Gold Board Act, 2025, gold buying, selling and exporting needs a licence from the Ghana Gold Board, and doing it without one is an offence. The Board buys gold from miners who are not large-scale. So a group should sell only to licensed buyers or to the Board itself. It is safer, and it leaves a record that a bank may one day ask to see.”

The Board buys gold from miners who are not large-scale.
So a group should sell only to licensed buyers or to the Board itself.
It is safer, and it leaves a record that a bank may one day ask to see.”

pages.text: That evening, Doris helped her uncle write a formal letter. At the top right she wrote his address, House 12, Dunkwa Road, Akim Oda, and below it the date, 14th March, 2027. On the left: The District Officer, Minerals Commission, District Office, Akim Oda. “Dear Sir,” it began, and the heading read: REQUEST FOR GUIDANCE ON APPLYING FOR A SMALL-SCALE MINING LICENCE AS A GROUP. The body read: “I am writing on behalf of six small-scale miners who wish to work lawfully as one group. Firstly, we would like to know the documents and steps required. Secondly, we would like to know whether a cooperative programme is open to us. We shall be grateful for your kind guidance.” He ended with “Yours faithfully,”, signed, and wrote his full name, Kwabena Opare.

pages.text: The six men met on the bench outside the house and wrote rules in a notebook. One would be treasurer and keep every pesewa in a record. One would be safety officer. They would put some money together for helmets, boots and a water pump. They would never use children in the pits, and they would find out how to stop using mercury. “It may take months,” Uncle Opare warned. “And we may be refused.” Doris nodded. “But now you are one group with a plan, Uncle, not six men hiding,” she said.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: this is a full formal letter. It has the writer’s address, the date, the recipient’s designation and full address, “Dear Sir”, a heading, “Yours faithfully”, a signature and the writer’s full name. The body is polite and clear, gives two reasons and uses no contractions or slang. Remember that the law and the fees may change, so a real application should follow the district office’s current instructions. Check the eight features before you hand in a formal letter. The end.
